newsitem.title: POLAND: Debate rages on 15 years after Polish martial law.
newsitem.headline: Debate rages on 15 years after Polish martial law.

text.p: General Wojciech Jaruzelski is more sure than ever he was right to unleash martial law on Poland 15 years ago, although he admits the mass arrests went too far and says he deeply regrets the suffering that ensued.
"I am still deeply convinced this decision was essential given the internal and especially external realities of the time," the former communist leader told Reuters on Thursday.
By December 1981, Poland was in turmoil, with the communist party's monopoly of power threatened by the rise of Solidarity, the Soviet bloc's first free trade union.

The Soviet Union, which had not hesitated to use force to suppress an anti-communist uprising in Hungary in 1956 and the liberal "Prague Spring" in 1968, was facing a renewed threat to its hegemony in Eastern Europe.
On the freezing night of December 12 to 13, Polish security forces raided homes nationwide, often brutally dragging off supporters of Solidarity.
Days later police fired on resisting workers at two coal pits in southern Poland, killing nine men at one mine.
A nationwide curfew was imposed, phones were cut then censored, Solidarity banned and the media rigidly curbed.
Up to 10,000 people were interned long-term, and many more hauled in and threatened by police during the one and a half years of martial law, followed up by a period of repression.

Jaruzelski argues he acted to avert a Soviet-led invasion which would have led to a greater catastrophe and says his action paved the way for change when the Soviet transformation at the end of the 1980s made it possible.
An opinion survey by the public CBOS institute published on Thursday suggested that a majority of Poles -- now living in a democracy with a fast-growing economy -- agree with him.

It showed that 54 percent consider the martial law decision was correct, 30 percent view it as wrong, with 16 percent undecided. Among the same 1,134 adults, only 22 percent said they had approved it in 1981, while 58 percent disapproved.

"People have seen that the martial law was a kind of purgatory which allowed us to get through those difficult years to a situation where it was possible to resolve our problems differently," commented Jaruzelski, 73, who in 1989 presided over the communists' surrender of power.

But debate prompted by the anniversary highlighted the continued divisions in Poland, where ex-communists hold the government and presidency but are being challenged by Solidarity-rooted parties in elections due next year.
The then Solidarity leader, ex-President Lech Walesa, said the CBOS poll reflected a communist propaganda success in pushing the line that martial law had been a "lesser evil".
"By introducing martial law, the communists shattered the hope that was flowering among the people," said Walesa, adding: "I don't judge the general. History will judge him."

"If we had begun reforming our state then, we would long ago have been in NATO and European structures. We wasted the greatest historic opportunity and instead of making a leap towards civilisation, we regressed," he told Reuters in Gdansk.
Many analysts argue Moscow would not have invaded in 1981, and the Polish communists acted merely to cling to power.
Jaruzelski said several Western and ex-Soviet leaders had later told him they considered his martial law action justified, but he admitted to mistakes in 1981 and later.
"Looking back, the scope of internment was too wide, there were local settling of scores, where people were interned who should not have been...and I greatly regret this," he said.
Jaruzelski said that after martial law Poland's communist leadership long included conservatives who hindered reforms.

"I didn't have good information...on various Solidarity people who were presented to me as demonic figures and who proved to be worthy of respect, with whom it was possible and necessary to find a common language and joint understanding."
Jaruzelski said the colliery shootings had been a tragic accident that had gone against his intentions.

The left-dominated parliament in October voted that Jaruzelski and other communist leaders should not be prosecuted over martial law, but he still faces trial in Gdansk over the shooting by security forces in 1970 of dozens of demonstrators.
